title: Lifetimes
summary: 'a names how long a borrow lives, letting a signature tie its output to its inputs.
lecture: Every reference has a lifetime - the region of code it's valid for. Usually the compiler tracks these silently. Lifetime ANNOTATIONS ('a) exist for signatures where the relationship between references can't be inferred: they are names that declare 'these references live at least as long as each other'.

The classic case: a function returns a reference that could point into either of two inputs. The signature fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str says 'the result borrows from a or b, so it stays valid only while BOTH do'. At each call site, 'a becomes the shorter of the two input lifetimes.

Annotations never change how long anything lives - they only describe constraints so the compiler can check callers. If you can't write the relationship down, the design usually wants an owned return type instead.

example.caption: One lifetime parameter ties the returned borrow to both inputs.
